title: Unit 5: Organisation and Inventory
text:
Why this matters
A farm is a busy workplace. If tools are left lying around, materials are poorly stored, or tasks are not logged, it becomes harder to work safely and efficiently. Good organisation protects people, equipment, and the wider farm environment.

title: Unit 5: Organisation and Inventory
Unit 5: Organisation and Inventory
text:
Equipment

broom or brush
gloves
notebook or checklist
labels or marker if available

title: Unit 5: Organisation and Inventory
text:
Before you start

Walk through the area first and identify hazards.
Keep walkways clear.
Handle heavy items carefully.
Report broken equipment or obvious safety risks.

title: Unit 5: Organisation and Inventory
text:
Task 1: Great tidy-up
{width:60%}

Barn and shed organisation

Sweep the floors and clear any debris.
Return tools to their proper hooks or racks.
Check that all tools are accounted for.
Wipe down work surfaces.
Organise shelves and storage areas.
Stack bags and containers neatly.
Remove rubbish to the correct bin.



Organisation principles

A place for everything and everything in its place.
Most-used items should be easiest to reach.
Heavy items should be stored lower down.
Label storage areas clearly.
Keep walkways and exits clear.

title: Unit 5: Organisation and Inventory
section: Task 2: Wood pile and pot storage
text:
Task 2: Wood pile and pot storage
{width:60%}

Wood pile management

Re-stack the wood pile so it is stable and safe.
Keep wood stacked in rows and away from buildings where possible.
Remove rotten or unsafe pieces.
Leave air gaps for drying and ventilation.



Pot sorting and storage

Sort pots by size.
Stack pots of the same size inside each other.
Remove broken pots or damaged items.
Store pots neatly so they do not block access.

title: Unit 5: Organisation and Inventory
text:
Task 3: Tool audit and maintenance
Proper tool maintenance extends tool life and improves safety:

Clean dirt, mud, and plant material from tools.
Wipe metal tools if they are rusty or damp.
Check wooden handles for splinters or damage.
Hang tools on their designated hooks or racks.
Coil hoses neatly and store them safely.
Place sharp tools where they cannot be knocked over or reached by accident.

title: Unit 5: Organisation and Inventory
text:
Task 4: Security and final sweep
Before leaving the area:

Lock shed doors and secure gates if required.
Close windows and doors.
Check for trip hazards.
Turn off water taps or other equipment if needed.
Conduct a final visual sweep of the area.

title: Unit 3: Restoration and Tree Health
text: This unit focuses on restoration work and long-term care of young trees. Students learn that healthy ecosystems are built through ongoing care, especially in places where invasive weeds and grazing pressure can slow recovery.

text: This unit focuses on restoration work and long-term care of young trees. Students learn that healthy ecosystems are built through ongoing care, especially in places where invasive weeds and grazing pressure can slow recovery.

title: Unit 3: Restoration and Tree Health
text:
Why this matters
Restoration planting is a long-term commitment. A young tree can fail if it is crowded by weeds, damaged by grazing, or left without support. Regular monitoring helps ensure the farm becomes a more resilient and biodiverse place over time.

title: Unit 3: Restoration and Tree Health
Unit 3: Restoration and Tree Health
text:
Equipment

heavy-duty gloves
loppers or secateurs
notebook or clip board
boots suitable for rough ground

title: Unit 3: Restoration and Tree Health
text:
Before you start

Wear thick gloves and sturdy footwear.
Watch your footing on slopes and uneven ground.
Work carefully around young plants so you do not damage them.
Never work alone in a remote or steep area.

title: Unit 3: Restoration and Tree Health
text:
Task 1: Remove invasive gorse

Control invasive gorse to protect native plantings:

Put on heavy-duty gloves and collect the loppers.
Work around the hillside or restoration area carefully.
Cut gorse back to the base and pile it neatly for disposal.
Focus first on gorse close to young trees.
Keep the cut material away from tree guards.


Why this helps
Gorse competes strongly with native plants for light, space, and water. Removing it gives young natives a better chance to establish.

title: Unit 3: Restoration and Tree Health
section: Task 2: Conduct a young tree audit
text:
Task 2: Conduct a young tree audit
Check on newly planted trees to ensure their survival:

Walk the farm perimeter and inspect each planted tree.
Check whether the tree is alive and whether the guard is secure.
Remove grass and weeds inside the tree guard.
Straighten leaning stakes and tighten loose ties.
Note any trees that need replacement.


Signs of a healthy tree

green leaves or buds
flexible stems
healthy bark
upright growth



Signs of stress or failure

brown or drooping leaves
brittle stems
damaged bark or broken ties
guard leaning or rubbing the stem

title: Unit 3: Restoration and Tree Health
text:
Recording observations
Help track restoration progress:

Count the number of trees checked.
Record how many trees are thriving, struggling, or dead.
Note any problem areas or repeated damage.
Take photos if there are clear changes.

title: Unit 3: Restoration and Tree Health
text:

Why is restoration more than just planting trees?
How do invasive weeds affect native plant survival?
What does a healthy restoration area look like?

title: Unit 1: Animal Care and Observation
text: This unit introduces students to the daily care of farm animals. It combines practical animal husbandry with observation, responsibility, and safe practice. Good animal care is not only about feeding and watering; it is also about noticing the small signs that suggest an animal is stressed, unwell, or behaving normally.

title: Unit 1: Animal Care and Observation
text:
Why this matters
Animals on the farm depend on people to provide safe water, appropriate feed, clean conditions, and careful monitoring. Regular observation helps identify health issues early and makes the farm a safer, calmer, and more productive place for everyone.

title: Unit 1: Animal Care and Observation
Unit 1: Animal Care and Observation
text:
Equipment

clean water container or hose
feed scoop or bucket
bedding material

title: Unit 1: Animal Care and Observation
text:
Before you start

Approach animals calmly and quietly.
Wash hands before and after handling animals or equipment.
Never chase, corner, or frighten animals.
If an animal appears injured or very distressed, inform the supervisor immediately.

title: Unit 1: Animal Care and Observation
text:
Task 1: Visit the chicken area



Chicken area


Follow these steps carefully when visiting the hen house:

Move quietly and slowly into the hen house.
Top up the water container with fresh water if needed.
Fill the feeder using the grain from the outside bin.
Check the birds for unusual behavior, feather loss, limping, or lethargy.
Note whether the hens are alert, active, and calm.
Optional: gently pat a chicken only if the bird is comfortable and the supervisor agrees.


What to look for

bright eyes and alert posture
steady movement and normal feeding
no obvious injuries or discharge
no repeated loud distress calls

title: Unit 1: Animal Care and Observation
text:
Task 2: Check paddock animals



Paddock animals


Ensure paddock animals have clean water, fresh bedding, and food:

Scrub out the water trough and refill it with clean water.
Spread fresh wood shavings in the shelter bedding area.
Place a scoop of nuts or feed in the wooden trough.
Check fencing, gates, and shelter areas for safety.
Observe animal movement and behaviour from a calm distance.
Report any injury, escape, or unusual behavior.


Good practice

Keep your voice low.
Avoid standing between an animal and its escape route.
Give animals space and respect their body language.

title: Unit 10: Kaitiakitanga and Kōura
text:
This 7-week unit introduces Year 9/10 students to the freshwater crayfish or kōura (Paranephrops zealandicus) as a taonga species and a practical case study in stream ecology, agriculture, and data investigation. Students explore how land use, riparian shade, water temperature, and habitat complexity affect kōura survival and growth.
The unit links field science with mathematics by asking students to collect, organise, compare, and interpret data. It also builds cultural understanding through kaitiakitanga, mātauranga Māori, and the idea of mahinga kai.

title: Unit 10: Kaitiakitanga and Kōura

Why this unit matters

Kōura are an important native species in Aotearoa New Zealand waterways.
Their survival is strongly affected by stream temperature, water quality, and habitat condition.
Field observations help students understand how farming, stream margins, and riparian planting influence freshwater health.
The unit provides a strong foundation for later statistical work such as bivariate investigations and evidence-based recommendations.

Week 1: Meet the kōura

title: Unit 7: Weather, Forecasting, and Environmental Impacts (Dunedin and Kaikorai Valley)
section: 1. Local Weather Context: Dunedin and Kaikorai Valley
text:
1. Local Weather Context: Dunedin and Kaikorai Valley

Why local context matters
Dunedin weather can change quickly due to coastal influence, wind shifts, and temperature differences between low and elevated areas. Kaikorai Valley can experience:

Cooler overnight temperatures and morning dampness.
Wind funnel effects in exposed areas.
Fast shifts between calm and gusty conditions.
Localized rain intensity that affects drainage and muddy zones.



Quick climate features to watch

Wind direction and strength (especially strong southerlies).
Rainfall intensity and duration.
Overnight minimum temperature and frost risk.
Daily maximum temperature and heat stress risk.
Humidity and dew point for disease pressure in plants.

title: Unit 7: Weather, Forecasting, and Environmental Impacts (Dunedin and Kaikorai Valley)
text:
2. Forecasting for Farm Decisions

Forecast checklist (daily)
Before starting practical work, check:

Next 24-hour rainfall forecast.
Wind forecast (speed and gusts).
Temperature range (min and max).
Any weather warnings (heavy rain, strong winds, cold snaps).
Air quality trend if available for the day.



Practical forecast actions

Heavy rain expected: delay soil disturbance and protect exposed soil.
Strong wind expected: secure loose materials, postpone spraying, check shelter access.
Frost risk expected: protect sensitive plants and adjust irrigation timing.
Hot, dry period expected: prioritize watering and check animal shade/water supply.

title: Unit 6: Practical Skills Refraction - Refractometer Unit (Year 9-10)
text:
Source resource and core concept
This unit is built from the worksheet in resources/Practical Skills Refraction 2026.pdf.

Core science idea from the worksheet

Light bends (refracts) when it moves between substances such as air, water, glass, or plastic.
Different amounts of dissolved substances bend light by different amounts.
Sugar is one dissolved substance we can test in food juices.
A refractometer measures sugar content in Degree Brix (% sucrose equivalent).
Higher Brix generally indicates greater sweetness and, in many crops, greater ripeness.



Why this matters on a farm

Farmers can estimate ripeness and harvest timing.
Brix helps compare crop quality across paddocks, varieties, and seasons.
Results support decisions about eating quality, processing, preserving, and market timing.

text: Detailed lesson plan

title: Unit 6: Practical Skills Refraction - Refractometer Unit (Year 9-10)
text:
Lesson 1: Refraction and refractometer setup
Time: 50 min
Learning intention: Understand how light refraction allows sugar measurement.
Success criteria: Students explain Brix and correctly calibrate the instrument.

Lesson flow

Hook and context (10 min)


Show refractometer and explain farm use.
Prompt: Why might farmers care about sugar levels?


Teach concept (10 min)


Light bends between materials.
More dissolved solids change refraction and shift reading.
Degree Brix = approximate percent sucrose equivalent.


Safety and handling (10 min)


Carry device with two hands.
Never scratch prism plate.
Clean with soft tissue and distilled water only.
No sharing droppers between unknown liquids without rinsing.


Calibration practical (15 min)


Place distilled water on prism.
Close flap.
Read scale.
If needed, adjust top screw to zero (teacher supervised).


Exit check (5 min)


Students write one sentence: How does a refractometer use light?



Resources

refractometers
distilled water
droppers/pipettes
lens tissue/soft wipes
gloves and eye protection as required

title: Unit 6: Practical Skills Refraction - Refractometer Unit (Year 9-10)
section: Lesson 2: Sample collection and Brix testing
text:
Lesson 2: Sample collection and Brix testing
Time: 50-60 min
Learning intention: Follow a valid sampling procedure and collect reliable data.
Success criteria: Students gather 3 repeat measurements for each selected item.

Procedure (from source worksheet)

Select fruit/vegetables from around the farm.
Prepare juice using a juicer or fork-mash and squeeze method.

section: Lesson 1: Introduction to Farm Dogs (Classroom/yard, 50-60 min)
text:
Lesson 1: Introduction to Farm Dogs (Classroom/yard, 50-60 min)

Success Criteria
Students can:

Identify key traits of a working sheepdog.
Match common commands to expected dog actions.
Prepare an observation sheet for Friday’s practical lesson.



Materials

Whiteboard and markers
Printed copy of the observation table (below)
Clipboards (if heading outside for short movement demo)



Lesson Sequence

Hook (5 min):

Ask: “What makes a farm dog different from a pet dog?”
Gather ideas and sort into categories: behaviour, training, purpose.

Mini-teaching (10-15 min):

Roles of farm dogs: gathering, driving, holding, backing, and yard work.
Key welfare concepts: calm pressure, no rough handling, handler responsibility.

Commands and communication (10 min):

Introduce likely commands students may hear on Friday (e.g. stop, lie down, walk up, come by, away, steady).
Discuss why consistent commands matter for animal safety.

Movement mapping task (15 min):

In pairs, students draw a small paddock and plot where dog, sheep, and handler should stand to move sheep through a gate.
Share and compare different movement plans.

Prepare for Friday (10 min):

Hand out observation sheet and explain what students must record during Jess’s session.
Review class expectations for safe conduct around Jess and sheep.




Formative Check

Exit ticket: “One thing Jess will need to do on Friday” + “One safety rule I must follow.”

title: Unit 4: Farm Dogs & Working with Sheep
text:
Lesson 2: Practical with Jess (Friday, 50-60 min)

Success Criteria
Students can:

Observe and accurately describe Jess’s response to commands.
Explain how Jess’s position changes sheep movement.
Demonstrate safe and respectful behaviour around working animals.



Safety Brief (Start of lesson)

Stay behind the marked observation line unless invited forward.
No sudden movements, shouting, or approaching Jess without permission.
Follow teacher instructions immediately around livestock.
If unsure, step back and ask.



Practical Sequence

Re-cap and briefing (5 min):

Review previous lesson’s commands and safety expectations.

Jess introduction (5 min):

Brief profile: breed/type, age, training, daily farm roles.

Demonstration rounds (20-25 min):

Round 1: Basic control (stop/lie down/walk up).
Round 2: Directional work around stock.
Round 3: Moving stock toward a target point.
Students complete observation table during each round.

Student analysis (10-15 min):

Pairs compare notes and identify one “effective handler move” and one “effective Jess behaviour.”

Debrief (5-10 min):

Whole-class discussion: What did Jess do that most affected sheep direction and speed?




Quick Assessment Task
Students submit a short paragraph:
“Describe one command, Jess’s response, and the effect on sheep movement. Include one safety behaviour you followed.”

Lesson 1: Choosing the right autumn crop
Goal: Understand why autumn planting in Otago requires hardy crops and realistic expectations about growth.

Key teaching idea
Autumn planting in Otago is mainly about building roots and establishing plants before winter. Lower light levels, cooler air, and frost risk mean students must choose crops that can cope with slow growth and cold conditions.

title: Unit 8: Autumn Planting (Seedlings)
text:
Lesson 2: Germination and seed sowing
Goal: Sow seeds accurately and explain how germination works.

Key teaching idea
Seeds need water, oxygen, and suitable temperature to start growing. Warming mats help the soil reach a useful germination temperature, but students still need correct depth, moisture, and labelling.


Core science idea: W.O.T.

Water: activates the seed and starts internal processes
Oxygen: allows respiration so the embryo can release energy
Temperature: helps enzymes work efficiently so the seed can germinate



Practical instructions

Prepare seed trays or small pots with seed-raising mix.
Moisten the mix so it is damp, not saturated.
Sow seeds using the rule of thumb: about \(2 \times\) the seed diameter.
Cover lightly and mist gently.
Label each tray with crop name, date, and group.
Place trays on a warming mat or in a protected germination area.



Practical roles



Role
Responsibility




Tray prep
Fill trays evenly and moisten seed mix.


Sowing
Place seeds at correct depth and spacing.


Labelling
Record crop, sowing date, and group accurately.


Setup check
Confirm trays are tidy and placed correctly.





Timing (40-50 min)

0-10 min: Demonstration of W.O.T. and sowing depth.

text:
Lesson 3: Seedling care and hardening off
Goal: Identify healthy seedling conditions and prepare a plan for moving seedlings outdoors.

Key teaching idea
Warmth alone is not enough. Seedlings also need enough light, airflow, and careful watering. Before transplanting, they must be hardened off gradually so they can tolerate colder outdoor conditions.


Student activities

Inspect trays or example seedlings for signs of success or problems.
Identify risks such as:

leggy seedlings
overwatering
dry trays
poor labelling
damping off

Create a 5- to 7-day hardening-off schedule.
Complete a crop profile or transplant plan from the workbook.



Hardening-off sequence

Day 1-2: short sheltered outdoor exposure
Day 3-4: longer outdoor time with some cooler air
Day 5-6: most of the day outside if conditions are suitable
Day 7: ready for transplanting if roots, moisture, and weather are appropriate



Timing (40-50 min)

0-10 min: Review seedling care and common failure points.
10-20 min: Tray inspection and discussion.
20-35 min: Hardening-off plan task.
35-45 min: Crop profile or transplant recommendation.
45-50 min: Reflection and teacher check.



Success criteria

I can describe what a healthy seedling needs.
I can identify at least two common seedling risks.
I can make a realistic hardening-off plan.

title: Unit 1: Sector and Safety
text:
New Zealand Primary Industries

Key Vocabulary
Before diving into the activities, review the key terms below. You will need these to answer the questions in the following sections.
Biodiversity
The variety of plant and animal life in the world or in a particular habitat, a high level of which is usually considered important and desirable.
Horticulture
The branch of agriculture that deals with the art, science, technology, and business of growing plants (fruits, vegetables, flowers).
Pastoral Farming
Farming aimed at producing livestock (animals), such as dairy cattle, beef cattle, and sheep, rather than growing crops.
Primary Production
The sector of the economy involved in the extraction and production of raw materials, such as farming, logging, hunting, fishing, and mining.
Ruminant
A hoofed mammal (like a cow or sheep) that chews the cud and has a specialized stomach system to digest grass.

The Seven Key Sectors
Did you know? Primary production contributes billions of dollars to the New Zealand economy every year.
New Zealand’s primary industries are grouped into seven main sectors. Pastoral farming (Dairy, Beef, Sheep) is the largest, utilizing our grasslands. Horticulture covers fruit and vegetables, while Forestry manages timber. We also have Aquaculture / Seafood for fish, the Equine sector for horses, and Sports Turf management.

The production of milk and milk products is a major part of ____________________ farming.

The primary industries aren’t just about farming. There are thousands of different jobs available, from scientists and engineers to managers and technicians. Let’s explore some of the career opportunities.

text:
Focusing on Sustainability
As we learn about New Zealand’s primary industries, it’s vital to think about sustainability. This means managing our land, water, and resources in a way that is good for the environment, for people, and for the economy, both now and in the future. Let’s check your understanding of this important idea.

The main goal of sustainable farming is to…?

Produce the most food possible in one year.
Use the newest and most expensive technology.
Make sure we can farm successfully for many years without harming the environment.
Only farm plants and not animals.

Why is protecting biodiversity important for a farm?

It makes the farm look nicer.
It helps create a healthy ecosystem, which can improve soil and control pests naturally.
It is required by law in every single case.
It means the farmer can charge more for their products.

Which of these is an example of a sustainable practice on a farm?

Allowing cow manure and fertiliser to wash directly into rivers.
Planting native trees along stream banks to filter water.
Removing all trees to make bigger paddocks.
Using as much water as possible for irrigation.

How does using resources like water carefully help a farm in the long run?

It doesn’t help; using more is always better.
It ensures there will be enough water available for the farm in future dry years.
It makes the grass grow slower.
It is only important for farms near the ocean.



Sustainability Vocabulary
Thinking about safety and long-term success leads us to sustainability. This means using our resources wisely to ensure the primary industries can thrive for generations to come, protecting our environment. Match the sustainability terms from the word bank to their correct definitions below.
Word bank: Sustainability, Riparian Planting, Erosion, Ecosystem, Greenhouse Gas Emissions, Carbon Footprint

The practice of meeting our own needs without preventing future generations from meeting theirs. It balances environmental, social, and economic factors.
Planting trees and native plants along the banks of rivers, streams, and lakes to improve water quality and create habitats for wildlife.
The gradual wearing away of land surface (soil) by wind, water, or other natural agents, which can be accelerated by farming practices.
A biological community of interacting organisms (like plants and animals) and their physical environment.
Gases like methane (from livestock) and carbon dioxide that are released into the atmosphere and contribute to climate change.
The total amount of greenhouse gases generated by our actions, often related to an activity or an organisation.



Extension Questions

Question 2: Resource Management and Future-Proofing

Explain how using resources wisely (such as through riparian planting or smart irrigation) acts as a form of insurance for a farmer’s long-term success.
Connect the idea of a safe working environment to the broader goal of a sustainable and thriving rural community.

title: Unit 2: Garden and Berry House Maintenance
text:
Why this matters
Plants grow best when their basic needs are met consistently. Weeds compete for water and nutrients, poor watering can stress plants, and neglected seedlings can struggle to establish. By caring for the garden regularly, students support food production and learn sustainable horticultural practices.

Before you start

Check the weather before watering.
Avoid walking on wet soil where possible.
Remove weeds carefully so you do not disturb crop roots.
Ask for help if you are unsure which plants are crops and which are weeds.

title: Unit 2: Garden and Berry House Maintenance
text:
Task 1: Watering run

Proper watering is essential for plant health:

Use the blue bin supply to fill watering cans.
Deliver at least two full cans per raised bed.
Water the herb boxes by the barn if needed.
Water at the base of plants rather than over leaves.
Check soil moisture first; it should be damp but not soggy.


Watering tips

Water early in the morning or late in the afternoon when possible.
Seedlings need gentle watering so they are not displaced.
Different plants need different amounts; observe and adjust.

title: Unit 2: Garden and Berry House Maintenance
section: Task 2: Weed and tend the beds
text:
Task 2: Weed and tend the beds
Keep garden beds healthy and productive:

Collect gloves, a fork, and a wheelbarrow.
Remove weeds from vegetable beds and no-dig beds.
Gently aerate the topsoil if needed.
Remove dead or diseased plant material.
Check plants for pests, wilting, or poor growth.


Good weed control practice

Pull weeds from the root.
Avoid disturbing crop roots.
Add weeds to the compost pile if they are not seeding.

title: Unit 2: Garden and Berry House Maintenance

text:
Task 3: Care for the berry house

Maintain the berry house for healthy fruit production:

Weed around the base of the berry plants.
Apply a fresh layer of wood chips to suppress weeds and hold moisture.
Check berry plants for fruit development.
Remove dead canes or leaves carefully.
Make sure plants are still supported and not tangled.


Berry care notes

Keep mulch slightly away from stems.
Monitor for disease or pest damage.
Healthy berry plants usually show strong growth and good leaf colour.

title: Unit 2: Garden and Berry House Maintenance
text:
Task 4: Seedling care and propagation
Care for the next generation of plants:

Check the seed raising tray in the tunnel house.
Use a spray bottle to dampen the soil of emerging seedlings.
Remove any failed seedlings.
Transplant seedlings when they are ready.
Label trays clearly.


Seedling care reminder

Keep soil moist but not waterlogged.
Provide light and airflow.
Watch for damping off disease and overcrowding.

title: Unit 4: Environmental Observation
text:
Why this matters
Environmental observation helps us collect evidence about what is happening in a place. A stream, a patch of grass, or a bee hive can tell us a lot if we look carefully and record what we notice. These observations support environmental learning, stewardship, and practical decision-making.

title: Unit 4: Environmental Observation

binoculars if available
camera or phone for photos
timer
suitable footwear

title: Unit 4: Environmental Observation
text:
Before you start

Observe quietly and respectfully.
Do not disturb wildlife or enter unsafe areas.
Stay clear of bee hives and move calmly.
Record the date, time, and weather conditions each time.

title: Unit 4: Environmental Observation
text:
Task 1: Stream study

Water quality and flow are useful indicators of ecosystem health:

Note whether the water looks clear or murky.
Describe whether the flow is fast, slow, or still.
Look for signs of erosion, pollution, or debris.
Notice whether aquatic life or insects are visible.
Record bird calls, plant growth, or changes along the bank.


Helpful observation prompts

Is the water level high, normal, or low?
Is the area cooler or warmer than nearby open ground?
What signs of life can you see?

title: Unit 4: Environmental Observation
text:
Task 2: Bee watch
Monitor bee activity to understand colony health:

Stand to the side of the hive and stay clear of the flight path.
Maintain at least two metres distance.
Set a timer for 60 seconds.
Count how many bees leave the hive.
Count how many return in the same period.
Note weather conditions and whether bees are carrying pollen.


What the numbers can suggest

high activity may suggest a healthy active colony
low activity may relate to weather or possible stress
more returning than leaving may indicate a productive foraging period

title: Unit 4: Environmental Observation

Observe the bigger picture:

Note weather conditions such as wind, cloud cover, and temperature.
Record any birds, insects, or mammals seen.
Note which plants are flowering or fruiting.
Describe any seasonal change you notice.
Write an overall impression of ecosystem health.
